claims.text: Adding 0.5–1 wt% nanoscale Y2O3 to a MoNbTaW-based refractory high-entropy alloy by mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering will produce a uniform dispersion of Y2O3 nanoprecipitates.
Uniformly dispersed Y2O3 nanoprecipitates act as sinks for radiation-induced vacancies and interstitials.
Capture of vacancies and interstitials by Y2O3 nanoparticles reduces defect clustering.
Capture of vacancies and interstitials by Y2O3 nanoparticles reduces dislocation-loop formation.
Under 1 MeV Kr-ion irradiation at 500°C to 1 dpa, Y2O3 dispersion will reduce swelling relative to unmodified MoNbTaW-based alloy.
Under the specified irradiation conditions, Y2O3 dispersion will lower radiation-induced defect density relative to unmodified MoNbTaW-based alloy.
Under the specified irradiation conditions, Y2O3 dispersion will improve retention of hardness relative to unmodified MoNbTaW-based alloy.
Under the specified irradiation conditions, Y2O3 dispersion will improve retention of yield strength relative to unmodified MoNbTaW-based alloy.
Y2O3-mediated defect removal will maintain the alloy's phase stability.
Y2O3-mediated defect removal will maintain the alloy's inherent mechanical properties.
Irradiation with 1 MeV Kr ions at 500°C to 1 dpa simulates plasma-facing conditions in fusion reactors.
Maintaining a uniform Y2O3 nanoparticle distribution at high temperature is critical to the predicted improvement.
The appropriate experimental baseline is an unmodified MoNbTaW-based HEA exposed to identical irradiation conditions.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts benefit from a uniform Y2O3 dispersion, but the falsification rule additionally requires observation of a non-uniform or unstable dispersion. Consequently, a uniformly dispersed material showing no reduction in damage or no mechanical-property benefit would not unambiguously falsify the hypothesis as written.
